title: What is polymorphism really buying you?
summary: Beyond the mechanism — the actual maintenance win a candidate should be able to point at, not just "runtime dispatch."

slides.markdown:
"Runtime method dispatch" is a correct definition of polymorphism and a weak interview answer — it describes the mechanism without saying why anyone should care. The stronger answer names the payoff: callers stop needing to know or check what type they're holding.

This topic gives you the mechanism in one line, then the payoff with a concrete before/after so it's not just an abstract claim.

Ask: **"Do you want how it works, or what it actually buys you day-to-day?"** Most interviewers want both, but leading with this question signals you already know the two are different — the mechanism is dynamic dispatch, the payoff is what that dispatch enables for the people writing calling code.

See [polymorphism](polymorphism) for the full mechanism if a deeper dive into vtables and dispatch is warranted.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: mechanism in one line, then the payoff
slides.markdown:
One line for the mechanism: **calling the same method name on different objects runs each object's own version, decided at runtime.** Then the payoff, stated explicitly: **callers stop branching on type.** Instead of an `if/else` chain checking "is this a Circle, a Square, a Triangle..." at every call site, one call — `shape.area()` — works no matter which concrete type is underneath.

The payoff sentence is what most "runtime dispatch" answers skip, and it's the part that actually matters for maintainability.

This is [ocp-open-closed](ocp-open-closed) made concrete: the polymorphic version is open to a new `Pentagon` (just add the class) but closed to modification (no existing call site changes). The if/else version needs an edit everywhere the type check appears.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: what's the actual runtime cost?
slides.markdown:
A vtable lookup — one extra indirection to find the correct method implementation for the object's actual class, versus a direct call that's resolved at compile time. In practice this cost is small and usually invisible; modern JIT compilers can even eliminate it entirely in hot loops through **inline caching**, when the actual type at a call site turns out to be predictable at runtime.

The honest framing: it's a real, measurable cost in principle, but essentially never the bottleneck in practice — trading it away for a type-switch chain is rarely the right call for performance reasons alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: does this only apply to inheritance, or does an interface give the same thing?
slides.markdown:
An interface gives you the exact same payoff — callers still get one call site (`shape.area()`) regardless of which concrete implementation is underneath, and dispatch is still resolved at runtime via the object's actual type. Inheritance isn't required for polymorphism; it just happens to be one common way to get it.

In fact, many modern style guides prefer interface-based polymorphism specifically because it doesn't force the implementer to give up their one supertype slot — the payoff is identical, the cost profile is often better.

slides.sectionTitle: Weak answer: defining dispatch without naming the payoff
slides.markdown:
**Weak answer:** "Polymorphism means the same method call can behave differently depending on the object's actual type at runtime."

**Why it's weak:** this is a correct definition of the mechanism, and nothing more — it doesn't say why that's useful, which is exactly what "buying you" is asking. An interviewer hearing only this can't tell whether you've ever actually felt the pain of the if/else chain it replaces.

**Correct model:** always close the mechanism sentence with the payoff sentence — callers stop branching on type, and new types slot in without touching existing call sites.

slides.sectionTitle: Wrong answer: polymorphism removes the need for any conditionals
slides.markdown:
**Wrong answer:** "Polymorphism removes the need for conditionals entirely — you should never type-check in well-designed code."

**Why it's wrong:** it's an overcorrection. Some conditionals genuinely aren't about dispatching on type at all — validating a range, checking a business rule — and forcing those into a class hierarchy just to avoid an `if` statement usually makes the code worse, not better. Polymorphism replaces conditionals that exist purely to pick behavior *by type*, not conditionals in general.

**Correct model:** the target is type-switch chains specifically, not every `if` statement in the codebase.

"Polymorphism means calling the same method name on different objects runs each object's own version, resolved at runtime. The real payoff is that callers stop branching on type — instead of an if/else chain checking every possible type at every call site, one call works no matter what's underneath. Adding a new type means adding one class, not editing every call site that used to type-check. It costs a small vtable lookup, which is essentially never the bottleneck, and it works the same whether you get it from inheritance or an interface."
